title: Time, Velocity, and Speed
lead: Motion takes time, and describing it needs more than where an object started and where it ended. This section defines time as change and elapsed time as the difference between two clock readings, then defines average velocity as displacement divided by the time of travel, instantaneous velocity as the velocity at one instant, and speed, which is the magnitude of velocity and carries no direction, so that a round trip can have a large average speed and an average velocity of zero.
objectives: Explain the relationships between instantaneous velocity, average velocity, instantaneous speed, average speed, displacement, and time.
Calculate velocity and speed given initial position, initial time, final position, and final time.
Derive a graph of velocity vs. time given a graph of position vs. time.
Interpret a graph of velocity vs. time.
summary_html:
• Time is measured in terms of change, and its SI unit is the second (s). Elapsed time for an event is $$\kdt = \ktf - \kto,$$ where $\ktf$ is the final time and $\kto$ is the initial time. The initial time is often taken to be zero, as if measured with a stopwatch; the elapsed time is then just $\kt$.
  • Average velocity $\kvb$ is defined as displacement divided by the travel time. In symbols, average velocity is $$\kvb = \frac{\kdx}{\kdt} = \frac{\kxf - \kxo}{\ktf - \kto}.$$
  • The SI unit for velocity is m/s.
  • Velocity is a vector and thus has a direction.
  • Instantaneous velocity $\kv$ is the velocity at a specific instant or the average velocity for an infinitesimal interval.
  • Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity.
  • Instantaneous speed is a scalar quantity, as it has no direction specified.
  • Average speed is the total distance traveled divided by the elapsed time. (Average speed is not the magnitude of the average velocity.) Speed is a scalar quantity; it has no direction associated with it.

figures.original_caption: A more detailed record of an airplane passenger heading toward the back of the plane, showing smaller segments of his trip.

During a 30-minute round trip to the store, the total distance traveled is 6 km. The average speed is 12 km/h. The displacement for the round trip is zero, since there was no net change in position. Thus the average velocity is zero.
Position vs. time, velocity vs. time, and speed vs. time on a trip. Note that the velocity for the return trip is negative.

exercises.prompt: A commuter train travels from Baltimore to Washington, DC, and back in 1 hour and 45 minutes. The distance between the two stations is approximately 40 miles. What is (a) the average velocity of the train, and (b) the average speed of the train in m/s?

parts.hint: The train ends up at the station it started from, so its displacement for the whole trip is zero.
The train covers 40 miles out and 40 miles back, 80 miles in 105 minutes; convert the miles to meters and the minutes to seconds.

answer.solution: (a) The average velocity of the train is zero because $\kxf = \kxo$; the train ends up at the same place it starts. (b) The average speed of the train is calculated below. Note that the train travels 40 miles one way and 40 miles back, for a total distance of 80 miles. $$\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} = \frac{80\ \text{miles}}{105\ \text{minutes}}$$ $$\frac{80\ \text{miles}}{105\ \text{minutes}} \times \frac{5280\ \text{feet}}{1\ \text{mile}} \times \frac{1\ \text{meter}}{3.28\ \text{feet}} \times \frac{1\ \text{minute}}{60\ \text{seconds}} = 20\ \text{m/s}$$

exercises.prompt:
A group of students has two carts, A and B, with wheels that turn with negligible friction. The two carts travel along a straight horizontal track and eventually collide. Before the collision, cart A travels to the right and cart B is initially at rest. After the collision, the carts stick together.
  1. Describe an experimental procedure to determine the velocities of the carts before and after the collision, including all the additional equipment you would need. You may include a labeled diagram of your setup to help in your description. Indicate what measurements you would take and how you would take them. Include enough detail so that another student could carry out your procedure.
  2. There will be sources of error in the measurements taken in the experiment both before and after the collision. Which velocity will be more greatly affected by this error: the velocity prior to the collision or the velocity after the collision? Or will both sets of data be affected equally? Justify your answer.

answer.solution: (a) Use tape to mark off two distances on the track — one for cart A before the collision and one for the combined carts after the collision. Push cart A to give it an initial speed. Use a stopwatch to measure the time it takes for the cart(s) to cross the marked distances. The speeds are the distances divided by the times. (b) If the measurement errors are of the same magnitude, they will have a greater effect after the collision. The speed of the combined carts will be less than the initial speed of cart A. As a result, these errors will be a greater percentage of the actual velocity value after the collision occurs. (Note: Other arguments could properly be made for ‘more error before the collision’ and error that ‘equally affects both sets of measurement.’)

exercises.prompt: Give an example (but not one from the text) of a device used to measure time and identify what change in that device indicates a change in time.

answer.solution: Any device that measures time does so by registering a change in some physical quantity, so the example should name both the device and the change. An hourglass, for example, measures time by the sand that has run from its upper bulb into its lower one, and the change is the level of the sand. A quartz watch counts the vibrations of a small crystal, a candle clock marks time by how far the candle has burned down, and a water clock by the level of water that has drained from a vessel. In each case it is the change, calibrated against a standard such as the second, that indicates that time has passed; without a change there would be no way to know.

exercises.prompt: There is a distinction between average speed and the magnitude of average velocity. Give an example that illustrates the difference between these two quantities.

answer.solution: Average speed is the distance traveled divided by the elapsed time, whereas average velocity is the displacement divided by the elapsed time, so the two differ whenever the path is longer than the straight line from start to finish. Any trip that turns back on itself will do. A runner who goes once around a 400 m track in 100 s has an average speed of 4 m/s, but she ends where she began, so her displacement is zero and so is the magnitude of her average velocity. A drive of 3 km to a store and 3 km back in half an hour has an average speed of 12 km/h and an average velocity of zero for the same reason. The two quantities agree only when the object moves along a straight line without reversing, so that the distance traveled equals the magnitude of the displacement.

exercises.prompt: Does a car’s odometer measure distance traveled or displacement? Does its speedometer measure speed or velocity?

answer.solution: The odometer measures distance traveled, since it adds up every kilometer the wheels roll through whatever the direction, and it keeps counting on a round trip that leaves the car with a displacement of zero. The speedometer measures speed, which is the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity, because it shows how fast the car is moving at that instant but gives no direction. Neither instrument records a direction, so neither one measures a vector.

exercises.prompt: If you divide the total distance traveled on a car trip (as determined by the odometer) by the time for the trip, are you calculating the average speed or the magnitude of the average velocity? Under what circumstances are these two quantities the same?

answer.solution: The odometer reading is the distance traveled, so dividing it by the time of the trip gives the average speed, not the magnitude of the average velocity, which would be the displacement divided by the time. The two are the same only when the distance traveled equals the magnitude of the displacement, that is, when the car moves along a straight line in one direction without turning back, so that its path is the straight line from where it started to where it finished. On any trip with a bend or a return leg the distance traveled is greater than the magnitude of the displacement, and the average speed is greater than the magnitude of the average velocity.

exercises.prompt: How are instantaneous velocity and instantaneous speed related to one another? How do they differ?

answer.solution: Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity, so the two have the same size at every instant. A passenger whose instantaneous velocity is −3.0 m/s toward the rear of the plane has an instantaneous speed of 3.0 m/s. They differ in that instantaneous velocity is a vector and has a direction, given in one-dimensional motion by its sign, while instantaneous speed is a scalar and has no direction and no sign. Two cars passing each other at 40 km/h in opposite directions have the same instantaneous speed but different instantaneous velocities.

exercises.prompt: (a) Calculate Earth’s average speed relative to the Sun. (b) What is its average velocity over a period of one year?

parts.hint: In one year, $3.16 \times 10^{7}$ s, the Earth goes once around a circle whose radius is the distance from the Earth to the Sun, $1.5 \times 10^{11}$ m by Table 1.3, so divide the circumference by the time.
After one year the Earth is back where it started, so its displacement for the year is zero.

exercises.prompt: The North American and European continents are moving apart at a rate of about 3 cm/y. At this rate how long will it take them to drift 500 km farther apart than they are at present?

On May 26, 1934, a streamlined, stainless steel diesel train called the Zephyr set the world’s nonstop long-distance speed record for trains. Its run from Denver to Chicago took 13 hours, 4 minutes, 58 seconds, and was witnessed by more than a million people along the route. The total distance traveled was 1633.8 km. What was its average speed in km/h and m/s?

parts.hint: Write the elapsed time in hours first: 13 hours, 4 minutes and 58 seconds is 13.083 h.
Divide the distance in meters by the elapsed time in seconds, or convert the answer in km/h with the factors for kilometers to meters and hours to seconds.

exercises.prompt: A student drove to the university from their home and noted that the odometer reading of their car increased by 12.0 km. The trip took 18.0 min. (a) What was their average speed? (b) If the straight-line distance from their home to the university is 10.3 km in a direction $25.0º$ south of east, what was their average velocity? (c) If they returned home by the same path 7 h 30 min after they left, what were their average speed and velocity for the entire trip?

parts.hint: The odometer gives the distance traveled; divide it by the time in hours.

The displacement is the straight-line distance, 10.3 km, in the direction $25.0º$ south of east; divide it by the same time, and the direction of the average velocity is the direction of the displacement.
The whole trip covers 24.0 km of road in 7.50 h.
The student is back home, so the displacement for the whole trip is zero.

exercises.prompt: Conversations with astronauts on the lunar surface were characterized by a kind of echo in which the earthbound person’s voice was so loud in the astronaut’s space helmet that it was picked up by the astronaut’s microphone and transmitted back to Earth. It is reasonable to assume that the echo time equals the time necessary for the radio wave to travel from the Earth to the Moon and back (that is, neglecting any time delays in the electronic equipment). Calculate the distance from Earth to the Moon given that the echo time was 2.56 s and that radio waves travel at the speed of light $(3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s})$.

answer.hint: The radio wave covers twice the distance from the Earth to the Moon in the echo time, so the distance is half of the speed multiplied by 2.56 s.

exercises.prompt: The planetary model of the atom pictures electrons orbiting the atomic nucleus much as planets orbit the Sun. In this model you can view hydrogen, the simplest atom, as having a single electron in a circular orbit $1.06 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}$ in diameter. (a) If the average speed of the electron in this orbit is known to be $2.20 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m/s}$, calculate the number of revolutions per second it makes about the nucleus. (b) What is the electron’s average velocity per revolution?

parts.hint: One revolution is the circumference of the orbit, $\pi$ times the diameter; the number of revolutions each second is the distance traveled each second divided by that circumference.
After one full revolution the electron is back where it started, so its displacement is zero.
